newsitem.title: USA: Los Angeles district attorney race remains tight.
newsitem.headline: Los Angeles district attorney race remains tight.

text.p: Los Angeles County District Attorney Gil Garcetti was winning his race for re-election by a razor-thin margin Wednesday but with thousands of absentee ballots still to be counted the outcome was far from certain.

In a race dominated by Garcetti's unsuccessful murder prosecution of former football star O. J. Simpson, he led challenger John Lynch, one of his own deputies, by 6,800 votes after more than 2 million ballots had been tallied.
But with the absentee vote from Tuesday's election still to be counted over the next few days, neither man was willing to declare victory or concede defeat.

Garcetti, possibly America's best-known district attorney as a result of the intense media interest in Simpson's criminal case, said he was "encouraged" by his slim lead but expressed frustration at the slow vote count.
"We feel very, very good where we are right now. I wish L.A. County would learn to do this much faster," he said.
Garcetti fell behind during the early vote count, getting 45 percent of the votes to Lynch's 55 percent. But Garcetti recovered to lead by 50.16 to 49.83 percent by daybreak.

Garcetti, who took office in 1992, is looking for a second four-year term as head of an agency with more than 1,000 prosecutors and a budget of $170 million. Although Simpson's trial thrust Garcetti into the national spotlight, the verdict in the case has dogged him throughout his campaign.

Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 in the murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman, is currently on trial in a wrongful-death civil suit brought by the victims' families.

Lynch, a political newcomer who heads the district attorney's Norwalk branch office, hammered away in his campaign at Garcetti's failure to obtain guilty verdicts, saying he had put incompetent prosecutors on the case.

Garcetti reportedly spent $1.3 million on his campaign, compared with Lynch's $350,000. Lynch accused the incumbent of offering voters "a million dollars of lies" in an intense and often divisive campaign.

Lynch also pointed to other high-profile embarrassments under Garcetti including a yearlong child-molestation investigation of pop star Michael Jackson that ended in 1994 without the filing of charges. Another blow came this year with the acquittal of rap star Snoop Doggy Dogg and his bodyguard on murder charges.
Garcetti countered in his campaign by portraying Lynch as an insensitive bureaucrat without Garcetti's own interest in such issues as spousal and child abuse.
